title: Ordination
hook: hands laid on, and prayer for the Spirit

segments.voice: Yesterday, weddings: vows made in the face of the congregation, naming the worse before it comes. Your line was for better, for worse. Did your note reach a couple? Day one thousand three hundred forty-seven.

Nobody in the church moves. At the front, a person in a plain white robe kneels on the stone floor with head bowed. The bishop steps forward and places both hands on that bowed head. Then, one after another, others come up and add their hands too, on the head, on the shoulders, until a small crowd of palms rests on one person. The silence stretches. Somebody coughs and is embarrassed about it. Then a prayer goes up, asking for the Holy Spirit to come on the one kneeling there. When the person stands up, the robe is the same. For the church, something has changed. Today: ordination.

Ordination is how a church sets someone apart for ministry. And at its center is a very old gesture: hands laid on, with prayer. It runs all through the book of Acts. First, helpers in Jerusalem. The apostles in Jerusalem need people to look after the widows' daily food, and the church chooses some. Then, in the King James Bible: "when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them." Prayer first, then hands. Second, a sending. In Antioch, the church is worshipping and fasting, and the Holy Spirit says, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them." And Acts says, "when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away." Notice who goes. Barnabas and Saul are already among that church's teachers. The hands don't keep them. The hands send them off. Third, a gift that needs tending. Paul reminds Timothy: "Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery." And in a second letter: "stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands." Stir it up, the way you'd stir a fire that's burning low. Fourth, where churches differ. Catholics and Orthodox call holy orders a sacrament: bishops ordain deacons, priests and other bishops, and they see a line of laid-on hands reaching back to the apostles. Anglicans keep bishops too. Other Protestant churches ordain ministers with hands laid on by other ministers or elders, as the church setting someone apart to serve. Quakers ordain no one at all. Churches also differ on who may be ordained. Where churches do ordain, hands and prayer tend to be at the center, as in Acts.

Here's the practice: pray for your minister. Settle, and breathe. If you have a pastor, a priest or a minister, bring them to mind: their face, their voice, the Monday after a long Sunday. If you don't, choose someone who has cared for your spirit in another way: a teacher, a grandparent, a friend who listens at two in the morning. Picture your hand resting lightly on their shoulder. If you pray, you can ask God to stir up the gift in them. If you don't, simply wish them strength for the work. The bell holds the time.
Ordination. A church setting someone apart for ministry, with hands laid on and prayer for the Spirit, and then sending them out.
Your line: hands laid on. Today, thank one person who has taught or cared for you, and tell them one specific thing they gave you. Day one thousand three hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: In Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches, a bishop ordains deacons, priests and bishops by laying on hands with prayer; other Protestant churches ordain ministers with the laying on of hands by other ministers or elders; Quakers do not ordain.

notes: Hook scene (bishop's hands, then other clergy adding theirs) resembles the ordination of priests in Catholic and Anglican rites; given as one scene, not universal. Confirm.
Acts 6 helpers described as helpers in Jerusalem (traditionally seen as the first deacons; the text itself does not use the title).
'Stir it up, the way you'd stir a fire': the Greek verb in 2 Timothy 1:6 (anazōpyreō) is often glossed 'rekindle'; the image is offered as a picture, not an etymology. Confirm.

Apostolic succession described as 'they see a line of laid-on hands reaching back to the apostles'; Anglicans 'keep bishops too' (Anglican understanding of succession is not elaborated). Confirm fairness.
'Many Protestant churches' and 'Quakers ordain no one at all' — confirm.
'Churches also differ on who may be ordained' is left general on purpose.

Editor pass: hook's 'something has changed' framed as the church's view, not the narrator's; 'many Protestant churches' softened to 'other'; sweeping 'the gesture is the same' replaced; 'every church' myth reworded.
